content: Your doctor has prescribed penicillin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will either be injected into a large muscle, such as your buttock or hip, or administered intravenously through a fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter. The infusion typically lasts 30 minutes or more and is given four to six times a day. Penicillin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, and infections of the skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and heart valves. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness of your treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Precautions Before Taking Penicillin: Inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to penicillin, cephalosporins, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially other antibiotics, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., naproxen, ibuprofen), atenolol, diuretics, oral contraceptives, probenecid, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, allergies, asthma, blood disorders, colitis, stomach problems, or hay fever. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking penicillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and regularly check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape. Avoid using Clinitest tablets, as penicillin may cause false-positive results. Administering Your Medication: Before administering penicillin, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your medication instructions precisely. Do not stop your treatment prematurely, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, stop the infusion and contact your healthcare provider immediately to ensure your therapy continues without interruption. Side Effects: Minor Side Effects: Penicillin may cause mild side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if these symptoms are severe or persistent: Upset stomach Diarrhea Severe Side Effects: Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following: Rash Itching Fever Chills Facial swelling Wheezing Difficulty breathing Unusual bleeding or bruising Dizziness Seizures Sore mouth or throat If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Storing Your Medication: If you are receiving penicillin intravenously, you will likely be instructed to store it in the refrigerator or freezer. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If additional penicillin is stored in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator for the next day’s use. Do not refreeze medications. If you are receiving penicillin intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide specific storage instructions. Store your medication as directed and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep all supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In Case of Emergency or Overdose: In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Signs of Infection: If you are receiving penicillin intravenously or subcutaneously, be aware of the symptoms of a catheter-related infection, which occurs at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin.
